text: The New Testament authors consistently misinterpreted the Hebrew Scriptures, wrenching passages from their original context to manufacture prophecies that supported their theological agenda.

Jesus did not fulfil Jewish messianic prophecy. The Hebrew Bible nowhere predicts a suffering, dying, and rising messiah; the early Christians retroactively read such ideas into texts that originally referred to Israel, David, or the Psalmist.
Paul abandoned Torah observance entirely, replacing the concrete ethical-legal framework of Judaism with a Hellenistic mystery religion centred on a dying-and-rising saviour figure.

The idea of bodily resurrection entered Jewish thought through Persian Zoroastrian influence during the Babylonian exile. Before this exposure, the Hebrew Bible knew only the shadowy existence of Sheol, with no concept of post-mortem vindication.

Matthew's citation of Isaiah 7:14 as a prophecy of the virgin birth is a deliberate mistranslation. The Hebrew word almah means simply 'young woman' and the passage in context refers to a child born during the reign of King Ahaz, not a miraculous conception seven centuries later.

The God of the Old Testament is a wrathful, tribal deity who commands genocide, while the God of the New Testament is a universal father of love. This fundamental contradiction reveals that the two testaments describe two different religious systems.

Early Christians abandoned the Sabbath, dietary laws, and circumcision — the three pillars of Jewish identity — demonstrating that Christianity was not a continuation of Judaism but a complete break from it.

The doctrine of the Trinity has no basis in the Hebrew Bible's strict monotheism. It represents a Hellenistic corruption of the original Jewish message about Jesus, imposed by Greek-speaking Gentile converts who could not grasp the simplicity of Jewish unitarianism.

Jesus' cleansing of the Temple was not a reform of existing institutions but a symbolic destruction of the Temple cult itself, signalling that the entire sacrificial system was obsolete and would be replaced.

The Epistle to the Hebrews presents a supersessionist argument that renders the Levitical priesthood, temple, and sacrifices permanently obsolete. Its author effectively declares the entire Old Testament religious system null and void.

The prophet Hosea's words 'Out of Egypt I called my son' originally referred to the nation of Israel at the Exodus, but Matthew repurposes them for Jesus' return from Egypt — a transparently contrived proof-text with no connection to the original meaning.

The extent to which the New Testament misrepresents the Old is evident in its treatment of the Suffering Servant of Isaiah 53. Critical scholarship agrees that the servant was originally Israel personified, yet Christians have insisted on reading Jesus into a text that had nothing to do with a future messiah.

Christianity is not the fulfilment of Judaism but a separate religion that emerged when a Jewish apocalyptic sect failed to persuade the majority of Jews and pivoted to a Gentile audience, discarding Jewish identity markers in the process.

The concept of Satan as a personal embodiment of evil is absent from the earlier books of the Hebrew Bible. The figure of 'the satan' in Job is a member of God's divine council, not a fallen angel. The dualistic cosmic battle of the New Testament reflects Persian and Hellenistic influence, not authentic Israelite religion.

Paul's allegorical reading of Sarah and Hagar in Galatians 4 is a classic example of early Christian eisegesis: he imposes a meaning on the Genesis narrative that its original author could never have intended, then uses it to argue for the displacement of the old covenant.

The New Testament's use of the Old is consistently tendentious. Where the Hebrew Bible speaks of collective Israel, the New Testament reads individual Christ; where the prophets denounce injustice, the evangelists find passion predictions; where the psalmist laments, the apostles discern resurrection proof-texts.

Jesus' reinterpretation of the law in the Sermon on the Mount — 'You have heard it said, but I say to you' — represents a fundamental break with Mosaic authority. He sets his own teaching above that of the Torah, a claim no Jewish prophet would have made.

The abandonment of the food laws in early Christianity, particularly Peter's vision in Acts 10, marks a decisive rupture with Judaism. What the Torah declared unclean for all time, the Christian movement summarily declared clean, severing one of the most basic distinctions of Jewish life.

The New Testament authors drew extensively on the Hebrew Scriptures, employing a range of interpretive strategies common in Second Temple Judaism. Their citation practices reflect both continuity with Jewish exegetical tradition and innovation driven by their conviction that Jesus fulfilled the scriptures.

Typological readings of the Old Testament, in which persons and events from Israel's history prefigure Christ and the church, represent one strand of early Christian interpretation. While some scholars treat typology as a legitimate hermeneutical category, others view it as a later imposition on texts that originally had different referents.

The development of resurrection belief in Second Temple Judaism is a complex subject. While some scholars have noted parallels with Zoroastrian concepts, the evidence suggests an internal development within Judaism, with antecedents in Ezekiel 37, Isaiah 26, and Daniel 12. The precise relationship between Jewish and Persian ideas remains debated.

Matthew's use of Isaiah 7:14 has been the subject of extensive discussion. The Septuagint translation, which Matthew appears to follow, renders the Hebrew almah with the Greek parthenos ('virgin'). Whether Matthew selected this reading because it served his theological purposes or because it reflected an existing interpretive tradition within Hellenistic Judaism is a question that divides commentators.

Paul's relationship to the Torah is more nuanced than the simple opposition sometimes alleged. In Romans, Paul affirms that the law is 'holy, righteous, and good' while also arguing that it cannot bring about the righteousness available through Christ. Scholars in the New Perspective tradition have argued that Paul's critique of the law was directed at its function as a boundary marker excluding Gentiles rather than at its moral content.

The question of continuity and discontinuity between the Testaments has shaped Christian theology since the second century. Marcion's radical rejection of the Old Testament was itself rejected by the early church, which insisted that the God of Israel and the Father of Jesus Christ are one and the same, and that the scriptures of Israel remain authoritative for Christian faith.

The use of Hosea 11:1 in Matthew 2:15 is often cited as an example of the evangelist's creative exegesis. However, some scholars have argued that Matthew is not proof-texting in the modern sense but rather reading the history of Israel as recapitulated in the life of Jesus — a typological approach that assumes rather than severs continuity between the testaments.

The relationship between early Christianity and the Jewish law varied across communities. The Jerusalem church, led by James, appears to have maintained Torah observance, while Pauline communities adopted a more flexible approach. This diversity suggests that the so-called 'parting of the ways' was a gradual and uneven process rather than a single decisive break.

The Suffering Servant of Isaiah 52–53 has been interpreted variously as a reference to Israel, the prophet himself, a righteous remnant, or a future messianic figure. The New Testament's application of this passage to Jesus belongs to a wider history of Jewish interpretation, which includes readings that identify the servant both corporately and individually.

The Epistle to the Hebrews presents Christ as the fulfilment of the Levitical priesthood and sacrificial system. Whether this constitutes supersession or fulfilment has been debated: some theologians argue that Hebrews' argument depends on the enduring validity of the Old Testament categories it employs, while others maintain that the epistle declares the old order definitively surpassed.

Scholarship on early Christian use of the Old Testament has moved beyond simple categories of 'correct' and 'incorrect' interpretation. Richard Hays' work on 'echoes of scripture' and Francis Watson's 'figural reading' have drawn attention to the creative and theologically motivated character of New Testament exegesis, situating it within the diverse interpretive practices of Second Temple Judaism.

The differences between the portrayal of God in the Old and New Testaments have often been exaggerated. The Hebrew Bible contains numerous affirmations of divine mercy and compassion alongside the judgment texts, while the New Testament includes warnings of judgment that rival anything in the prophets. The Marcionite dichotomy between a wrathful Old Testament God and a loving New Testament God is not sustained by a close reading of either corpus.
